title: Home Street North drainage swale: residents ask for a culvert; council studies it, then declines a fix costed at about $500,000
summary: Water from an open drain is designed to flow over Home Street North near Lowen Boulevard, leaving water and ice on the road. After an email from resident K.B. (Dec 2015), council asked administration to monitor and report; in Feb 2017 K.B. presented a petition asking for a culvert under the road, and council voted for a report with options and costs. The Dec 2017 report found a piped crossing would need the road raised about a metre, possibly property purchases, and cost roughly $500,000, so no fix was made; the city instead stepped up monitoring and maintenance.
status_detail: No reconstruction. Administration's Dec 5, 2017 report judged a culvert/bridge option unreasonable on cost and property impact; the mayor asked that the cost figures and the increased monitoring be relayed to the petitioners. The report asked for by the Feb 2017 motion was targeted for the summer 2017 study session but came to council in December. K.B. raised the swale again at the Aug 21, 2018 Maplewood hearing.
figures: Culvert/bridge option 'in the neighborhood of $500,000' plus likely property purchases (City Manager, 2017-12-05 1:24:16); mayor's paraphrase 'over $1 million', which the city manager called 'pretty, pretty close' (2017-12-05 1:27:59); road would need raising by about 1 metre per a mid-1990s review (2017-02-07 0:19:46).
reasons: cost: A piped crossing would be extremely costly (about $500,000) and require buying property. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); engineering-standard: Configuration inherited from the 1960s/1990s; raising the road about 1 m would affect neighbouring properties. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); already-doing: Public Works gives the spot extra monitoring and maintenance; 'not a perfect solution' but the best possible. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); cost: Inherited from Hanover; 'we wouldn't design it that way now', but correcting it would cost over $1 million. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Resident K.B. (an environment officer who lives on Home Street) wrote in Dec 2015 and presented a residents' petition on Feb 7, 2017: water backs up after every rainfall and can last weeks, ice builds up, vehicles lose parts in the dip, pedestrians walk through water; he called draining water over a road 'small-town thinking' and warned of liability if someone is hurt (claim, not tested).
mover: a Councillor Penner (Susan or Cari; not identified in the transcript)
vote: carried (count not recorded); Dec 2015 report request was by consensus
notes: Report requested Feb 2017 for the summer study session; it reached the public agenda Dec 5, 2017. The 2017 motion's mover is a Councillor Penner whose first name the transcript does not give. The Dec 5, 2017 video is audio only.

title: Old sewer and water mains replaced through street reconstruction (Barkman Avenue 2016, Oak Crescent and 4th Street 2017)
summary: Council approved Barkman Avenue (Main to Henry) as a 2016 local improvement replacing surface works, water main and sewer main at the end of their life, part of what the mayor called a long-term strategy to renew underground infrastructure before problems occur. The City Manager's 2017 annual report listed about $4 million of core infrastructure including underground sewer and water lines on Oak Crescent and 4th Street. Engineering for each year's capital works is contracted in advance (Blackburn/SBC, 2016 and 2018).
status_detail: Barkman first and second readings carried Dec 15, 2015 (one objector; Municipal Board borrowing approval required). 2017 sewer/water line work reported done (2018-02-06). 2019 engineering contract awarded Sept 18, 2018 (R18-211).
figures: Barkman: $2.14M total, $1M borrowed over 5 years, $840,000 Canada-Manitoba Infrastructure Program, $300,000 Municipal Road Improvement (City Manager, 2015-12-15 0:06:22); 2017 core infrastructure nearly $4M (annual report, 2018-02-06 0:04:58); 2019 engineering contract $376,580 (minutes R18-211); $753,791.63 of mostly storm sewer piping and concrete cut from the secondary water supply tender to fit the budget (2018-02-20 0:08:47; minutes R18-032).
reasons: already-doing: Planned renewal keeps the city ahead of problems and reduces sporadic maintenance. (Chris Goertzen)
public: One registered objection to the Barkman local improvement (not read into the record).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (first reading; identified as 'Councilor Swiper', medium)
notes: Barkman project completion is implied by later references but not confirmed from minutes (none for 2016).

title: Neighbours fear sewer backups from a 24-32 unit building on Hanover Street; staff say the line is sized for it
summary: At a conditional-use hearing for multi-family buildings on Hanover Street, neighbours said the 60-year-old sewer had already needed a plumber and asked whether many more units would make it back up into their homes. The City Manager said gravity mains are designed for future loading and this line is appropriately sized; the mayor said the whole system is televised about every 10 years. Council approved the conditional use.
status_detail: Sewer capacity was not treated as a reason to refuse; the conditional use and the variation were approved the same evening.
figures: System inspected by camera about every 10 years (mayor, 0:32:42); proposal 24 to 32 units replacing 3 houses (transcript).
reasons: not-grounds-to-block-development: Gravity mains are designed for future connections; engineering checks capacity. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); already-doing: Every part of the system is camera-inspected about every 10 years and renewed citywide, not charged to the neighbourhood. (Chris Goertzen)
public: Hanover Street residents (initials not reliably identifiable from the diarization) said the sewer was about 60 years old and asked if it would back up on the older side.
notes: Speaker labels for residents in this hearing are merged with the applicant's, so no resident is quoted.

title: Resident's repeated drainage complaint at Lowen Boulevard and Old Tom Road: provincial drain, no city work
summary: Resident R.F. wrote again about water pooling on low-lying lots along Old Tom Road at Lowen Boulevard. Staff said the drain is under provincial jurisdiction, culverts are as required, and improvements would come only if development prompts them. Deputy Mayor John Fehr said the Seine-Rat River Conservation District was in talks with the golf course downstream and that the water had to be dealt with downstream first.
status_detail: Letter received; no city action. Councillors asked that the resident be told about the downstream talks; the chair said they were only at the dialogue stage.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: The drain is a provincial drain maintained by the Province. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); private-property: The private lots are low-lying, on an old creek bed; improvements happen when development prompts them. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); study-first: Conservation district must deal with the water downstream (golf course) before this corner. (John Fehr)
public: R.F. (resident at Lowen Boulevard and Old Tom Road) had written to council before about water accumulating on his property.
notes: A Councillor Penner (female; first name not given) asked whether the conservation district could help; not attributed by name.

title: Council lets a commercial subdivision use roadside swales instead of curb, gutter and storm sewer, against staff advice
summary: Developers of the Steinbach North C-3 commercial subdivision asked to build swale (ditch) drainage with no curb and gutter instead of the city standard of curb-and-gutter or land-drainage sewer. Council deferred it on Apr 5, 2016 for a staff report; on May 3, 2016 it approved a one-time exception through the development agreement (gravity sewer, piped water, 32-foot concrete street, swale drainage). The City Manager warned it was a downgrade to a rural profile and would set a precedent.
status_detail: Exception approved for this development only (motion carried May 3, 2016). Zwaagstra said he would vote against; the full count was not stated.
reasons: fairness-precedent: Every future developer would expect the same exception; specs apply city-wide. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); fairness-precedent: Would make open ditches standard practice in commercial zones. (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: Affordable lots and attracting business outweigh the spec; swales work fine in industrial parks. (Jac Siemens / Cari Penner)
public: Delegates for the developer (named businessmen) argued swales handle 100-year events and recharge groundwater; not independently checked.
vote: carried (count not recorded; Zwaagstra stated he would vote against)
notes: Topic is drainage standards for new development, not backups. Mayor Goertzen did not chair this item (Deputy Mayor Fehr did); his vote is not known.

title: Water and sewer rates raised to cover system costs (Bylaw 2064; sewer rate up 11% in 2018)
summary: Council gave first reading to new water and wastewater rates in May 2016 and sent them to the Public Utilities Board; after PUB approval it passed Bylaw 2064 on Mar 6, 2018. Councillors said rates must cover what the service costs, including future upgrades.
status_detail: Bylaw 2064 second reading R18-050 (S. Penner / Zwaagstra) and third reading R18-051 (Siemens / Funk), both unanimous.
figures: About $1/month more per average residential customer in each of 2018-2020 (City Manager, 2018-03-06 1:00:07); sewer rate +11% in 2018 (2018 financial plan presentation, 0:00:58); 2016 increases water 4.8%, sewer 1.6% (2016 financial plan, 0:01:21).
reasons: user-pay: Rates must pay to keep the system operating and for future upgrades. (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Rates fund the utility generally; no backup-specific spending was tied to them in this period.

title: Councillor Susan Penner asks whether drainage should be built for rare major storms or average rainfall
summary: In her opening remarks on June 7, 2016, Susan Penner said Steinbach has invested significantly in drainage but sits on very flat land, so 'the rare but major storm' overwhelms the system, and asked whether infrastructure should meet the worst case or average precipitation with a buffer.
status_detail: A reflection, not a motion; no policy change followed in this period.
reasons: extreme-storm: Flat geography means rare major storms exceed the system. (Susan Penner); cost: Question of how much government should spend to mitigate rare events. (Susan Penner)

title: Fly-In Golf Course says city development is sending more water its way; asks for partnership and compensation
summary: On July 5, 2016 the Steinbach Fly-In Golf Course (delegate J.S.) told council that development in and around the city had changed water flows onto the course, and asked for an active partnership on water management, compensation for costs incurred, and an agreement to fund future damage (it cited about $48,000 a year in lost revenue from closures). The mayor said new subdivisions must have net-zero outflow under provincial rules but that much of the water comes from the neighbouring municipality; Councillor Fehr said conservation-district talks on retaining water upstream had stalled.
status_detail: No public decision granting compensation or a water partnership was found. Councillors later said (Dec 5, 2017) that a $500,000 grant request from the course had been denied in a closed meeting; council instead bought 40 acres from the course for $500,000 over 3 years and leased it back for $1 a year (carried; Zwaagstra, Funk and one Councillor Penner spoke against). Supporters cited the course's flood-mitigation spending.
figures: Lost revenue about $48,000/yr from closures, about $23,500 in 2000 (delegation, 2016-07-05 0:35:12-0:35:31); course spent over $675,000 on flood mitigation (Siemens, 2017-12-05 1:03:07); land purchase $500,000 over 3 years, lease $1/yr (2017-12-05).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: The creek through the course is a provincial drain; asked whether the province should contribute. (John Fehr); engineering-standard: New subdivisions already must keep net-zero outflow (provincial requirement). (Chris Goertzen); not-city-water: Much of the water originates in the adjoining municipality; needs regional partnerships. (Chris Goertzen); study-first: Conservation district still deciding between retention on the course or upstream; talks stalled. (John Fehr)
public: Delegate J.S. (golf course board): water is standing where it never stood; the course cannot afford the infrastructure to handle the surplus; 'all the calculating in the world doesn't always dictate what water will do'. Claims about the share of water caused by city development were not quantified.
vote: requests referred to budget process; land purchase carried Dec 5, 2017 (count not stated)
notes: Link between the July 2016 water requests and the later $500,000 grant request/land purchase is inferred from the Dec 2017 debate, not stated as such. The land purchase vote was not counted aloud and there are no 2017 minutes; it is not listed in split_votes because the debate was about finances, not drainage.

title: Residents raise flooding and runoff at development hearings; council relies on lot-grading rules in development agreements
summary: At several hearings neighbours said land already floods and asked where new runoff would go: Albert Street backyard flooding every spring (Jul 2016), standing water south of a Main Street project (Sept 2017), Brandt Street flooding in rainstorms (Dec 2017), a neighbour's culvert and grading (Mar 2018), and backyard flooding and basement water near 404 First Street (Jun 2018). Staff and the mayor answered that every new development needs a site-servicing and lot-drainage review, settled in the development agreement.
status_detail: Drainage was not the deciding factor in these files: the Albert Street rezoning and Main Street and corner variances proceeded with drainage left to development agreements; 404 First Street was denied (R18-135/R18-136) on lot size, setback and traffic grounds.
reasons: not-grounds-to-block-development: Every new development gets a detailed review of site servicing and lot drainage. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); engineering-standard: Drainage plan worked out with engineering and written into the development agreement. (Chris Goertzen)
public: D.W. (Albert Street): the lot floods 'just about every spring' and water floods half his backyard; a resident near a Main Street project said yards are 'very, very wet' in a wet year; K.L. (Brandt Street) described flooding during rainstorms; a letter for neighbours of 404 First Street reported periodic backyard flooding and some water in the basement.
resolution_no: R18-059 (Mar 20, 2018 variance, Fehr / C. Penner); R18-135, R18-136 (Jun 19, 2018 denials, Siemens / Zwaagstra)
notes: Residents identified by initials where their names were stated; one Main Street neighbour (Sept 2017) is not named in the passage reviewed.

title: Staff recommend refusing a lot-line subdivision over drainage; council ties 3-3 and tables it
summary: A subdivision moving the line between 275 3rd Street and 4 Fernwood Bay was recommended for denial because of drainage patterns and future servicing; the city engineer said approval would need a professional lot-grading plan for the six surrounding lots. A motion to deny tied 3-3 (Councillor Siemens absent) and failed; council then tabled it.
status_detail: Tabled to a later meeting; no later decision was found in the transcripts (no 2016 minutes exist).
figures: Lot grading plan would cover 6 neighbouring lots (city engineer's report via City Manager, 0:09:56).
reasons: private-property: City cannot impose conditions on neighbouring private lots; neighbours usually work drainage out among themselves. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); engineering-standard: Hard to change drainage on existing lots; follow the city engineer. (John Fehr)
public: Applicants were present; no neighbour objections were read into the record in the passage reviewed.
mover: a Councillor Penner (not identified) - motion to deny
vote: tie 3-3, defeated; then tabled (moved Zwaagstra, seconded a Councillor Penner)
notes: Which Councillor Penner moved the denial, and the third vote on each side, could not be determined.

title: Council refuses to waive the lot drainage plan required of a homeowner; 'the policy stands'
summary: Resident R.C. wrote asking to be excused from the drainage plan required as a condition of his variance, which cost $2,000-$3,000. Staff said the city-wide drainage policy (15-20 years old) has always applied, and older neighbourhoods are where water spills between properties. Councillors Funk and Fehr said drainage is the most common complaint and the policy must be kept; the mayor asked staff to tell him the policy stands.
status_detail: No waiver; administration was asked to inform the resident.
figures: Drainage plan cost $2,000-$3,000 (mayor, 2016-09-20 0:23:54); policy in place about 15-20 years (City Manager, 0:23:37).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Waiving would undo the policy; problems would return in forty years. (Earl Funk); engineering-standard: Development affects water elsewhere; an engineered plan protects the owner too. (John Fehr)
public: R.C. (resident) found the drainage plan cost hard to accept and said he gets along with his neighbours.

title: Mayor flags lagoon expansion as the next big hurdle; 2007 expansion good for about 12-20 years
summary: Discussing the City Manager's 2017 annual report, Mayor Goertzen said the next major hurdle would likely be expanding the sewage lagoon. The City Manager said the last expansion (2007) gave about a dozen to 20 years of capacity and the city needs to work toward the next one.
status_detail: No project decision in this period.
figures: Last lagoon expansion 2007, about 12-20 years of capacity (City Manager, 2018-02-06 0:21:43).
notes: Wastewater treatment capacity; included because the scope covers capacity, not because a backup was linked to it.

title: Elmdale Drain rebuild ($850,000) put back into the 2018 budget after years of deferral
summary: Presenting the 2018 financial plan, Councillor Siemens said the Elmdale Drain reconstruction (about $850,000, funded from reserves) had been pulled from the budget for several years on council's direction to wait until development prompted it, and had now been put back in.
status_detail: Budgeted in the 2018 financial plan (R18-056, carried 4-3 for reasons unrelated to the drain). The 2019 Elmdale Drain tender was awarded Mar 5, 2019 to Hy-Way Construction for $657,530 (R19-049), outside this period.
figures: $850,000 from reserves (Siemens, 2018-03-20 financial plan hearing 0:18:11); tender $657,530 (minutes R19-049).
reasons: development-led: Earlier deferrals: build the drain only when development in the area prompts it. (Council (as described by Jac Siemens))
vote: 4-3 on the whole financial plan (against: Zwaagstra, S. Penner, Funk - golf course and grants reasons)
notes: The 4-3 financial-plan vote is not a drainage split, so it is not listed in split_votes.

title: First Street infill: neighbour cites past sewer backups; rezoning proceeds, larger-footprint variance refused 4-3
summary: At the May 1, 2018 hearing on rezoning six First Street lots for 18 townhouses with suites (By-law 2092), resident T.B. said the neighbourhood had seen major sewer backup and flooding and asked what the added fixtures would do. Zwaagstra quoted the engineer's report that the developer pays for any sewer upgrades; the mayor said engineering ensures adequate infrastructure. Second reading passed unanimously. The 15-foot front-yard variance failed 3-4, with Councillor Fehr citing runoff from more hard surface and basements flooded in past events.
status_detail: Rezoning got second reading (R18-090, unanimous), went to the Municipal Board (hearing Aug 27, 2018) and was confirmed in 2019 (R19-102). Variance V-2018-03 defeated May 1 (R18-091) and formally denied May 15 (R18-105). Sewer upgrades left to the development agreement.
figures: 36 units in phase 1 on 6 lots; resident estimated 504 plumbing fixtures vs 42 (resident T.B., 0:15:10).
reasons: not-grounds-to-block-development: Developer must pay for sewer upgrades; staff won't sign off if it causes direct flooding. (Michael Zwaagstra); not-grounds-to-block-development: Engineering checks infrastructure; developer pays. (Chris Goertzen); overland-runoff: Variances add hard surface and affect water flow in the city. (John Fehr)
public: T.B. (Donald Avenue): 'We have seen major sewer backup and flooding in our neighborhood in the past'; also raised traffic and schools.
mover: Susan Penner (rezoning and variance); John Fehr (May 15 denial)
notes: Label K is shared by several speakers in this file; the two Fehr turns are attributed from the chair's call immediately before and the content.

title: Maplewood 44-unit rezoning denied 5-1, with Home Street drainage among the reasons
summary: Residents objecting to rezoning Maplewood Street lots for 44 townhouses (By-law 2101) raised runoff, including K.B., who said the Home Street swale already gets too much water. Council denied second reading 5-1. Councillors Siemens and Funk named overland flows and Home Street drainage as reasons; Zwaagstra moved denial for lack of clarity in the plan; Susan Penner voted against denial.
status_detail: Second reading denied Aug 21, 2018 (R18-191), as objecting residents asked.
figures: 44 units in 4 blocks of 11; 49 notices of objection with 84+ signatures (resident D.M., 0:28:33).
reasons: overland-runoff: Size and asphalt would create higher overland flows; no plan yet for where water goes. (Jac Siemens); overland-runoff: Drainage already not working on nearby Home Street. (Earl Funk)
public: K.B. (Home Street): already too much water at the Home Street swale, plus sump water pumped from an apartment building (claim, not verified); C.R. (Albert Street) asked how runoff would affect her yard; D.M. presented objections citing water management and runoff.

title: Existing drain near Heritage Parkway formalized as a public drain (By-law 2106)
summary: Council acquired the land by consent and registered an existing drain beside the Bethesda Primary Healthcare Centre (Heritage Parkway, south to Lowen Boulevard) as a public drain.
status_detail: By-law 2106 first and second readings Sept 4 (R18-200, R18-201) and third reading Sept 18, 2018 (R18-217), all unanimous.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Cari Penner; Jac Siemens
seconder: John Fehr; John Fehr; Michael Zwaagstra
notes: Routine; included for completeness of drainage decisions.

title: Steinbach joins the new Seine Rat Roseau Watershed District; Jake Hiebert becomes its chair
summary: Council approved the province's proposal to turn the Seine-Rat River Conservation District into the Seine Rat Roseau Watershed District and passed the by-law to join it. Jake Hiebert, council's appointee since November 2018, became chair in spring 2020 and reported on regional retention and drainage projects that slow water to prevent downstream flooding.
status_detail: Proposal approved Mar 5, 2019 (R19-060); By-law 2142 first and second reading Jan 21, 2020 (R20-014, R20-015) and third reading Feb 4, 2020 (R20-023). Jake Hiebert reappointed each year 2019-2021; re-elected board chair (minutes 2021-11-16).
figures: District budget about $1.2M (transcript 2020-06-02 0:48:06); 42 acre-feet retention project (transcript 0:50:51).
mover: R19-060 and R20-014 Jake Hiebert; R20-015 Damian Penner; R20-023 Jake Hiebert
seconder: R19-060 Damian Penner; R20-014 Susan Penner; R20-015 Jake Hiebert; R20-023 Damian Penner
notes: Watershed work is regional (farmland retention, waterways) rather than city sewer capacity.

title: Elmdale Street rebuilt with new sewer and water lines, and the Elmdale Drain project tendered
summary: Council approved a local improvement plan to rebuild about 300 m of downtown Elmdale Street with complete underground replacement of sewer and water lines plus drainage works, then awarded the 2019 capital works tender and a separate 2019 Elmdale Drain project tender. Both drew no objections and passed unanimously.
status_detail: LIP By-law 2112 passed first and second reading Dec 18, 2018 and third reading Feb 19, 2019 (R19-040); the 2019 capital works tender (R19-048) and Elmdale Drain tender (R19-049) were awarded Mar 5, 2019. Damian Penner cited the completed downtown Elmdale Street work in the 2019 budget debate.
figures: Surface works $1.05M, $700,000 borrowed over 5 years (transcript 2018-12-18 0:10:50); 2019 capital works tender $2,616,156 to Hy-Way Construction (minutes R19-048); 2019 Elmdale Drain tender $657,530 to Hy-Way Construction (minutes R19-049); 2018 reserve schedule lists $850,000 for the Elmdale Drain (minutes 2019-03-19, R19-074).
public: No objections at the Dec 18, 2018 public hearing.
mover: R18-285 Michael Zwaagstra; R19-040 and R19-049 Jac Siemens; R19-048 Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: R18-285 Jac Siemens; R19-040, R19-048, R19-049 Damian Penner
notes: No transcript exists for Mar 5, 2019; the drain tender is from the minutes only. The minutes do not describe the scope of the Elmdale Drain project.

title: Public drain and stormwater detention pond for Lexington Village approved; pond later relocated
summary: For the Lexington Village subdivision council opened a public drain (By-law 2118) and passed a plan of works for a stormwater detention pond that doubles as green space (By-law 2119). In October 2019 it rezoned the original pond site after the developer moved the retention pond to the northwest corner on engineering advice.
status_detail: By-law 2118 first/second reading Mar 5 (R19-055, R19-056) and third reading Mar 19, 2019 (R19-071); By-law 2119 third reading Mar 19 (R19-072); rezoning By-law 2126 second and third reading Oct 1, 2019 (R19-190, R19-191). All unanimous.
reasons: engineering-standard: Relocating the pond as engineered was reasonable and lets the subdivision proceed. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The developer's representative (D.B.) said the pond was moved because it was easier from an engineering perspective and 'nothing being taken away'.
mover: R19-071 Jac Siemens; R19-072 and R19-190 Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: R19-071 Jake Hiebert; R19-072 Damian Penner; R19-190 Jac Siemens

title: Deerfield Middle detention pond and pathway built under budget
summary: Council awarded the tender for the Deerfield Middle detention pond and pathway, a stormwater pond long in the capital plan, to the low bidder recommended by the city's engineer WSP. Jac Siemens noted it came in about $120,000 under budget.
status_detail: Tender awarded unanimously (R19-064).
figures: $588,550 plus GST to Friesen Hauling and Excavating, 7 bids; funded from the capital development reserve and gas tax reserve (transcript 0:31:57; minutes R19-064).

title: Sewer rate rises of 8.5% (2019) and 9.5% (2020) under the 2018 PUB-approved rate plan
summary: The 2019 and 2020 financial plans kept water rates flat but raised the wastewater (sewer) rate by just over 8.5% and then 9.5%, as previously approved by the Public Utilities Board under By-law 2064 (2018). In April 2020 council re-confirmed that by-law's phased rate dates.
status_detail: 2019 plan adopted (R19-063, unanimous); 2020 plan adopted and By-law 2064 rate schedule re-confirmed (R20-074, R20-078, unanimous). The rate plan expired at the end of 2020 (see 2022-water-wastewater-rates-bylaw).
figures: Sewer rate +8.5% in 2019 (transcript 2019-03-19 0:10:37); wastewater rate +9.5% in 2020 (transcript 2020-04-07 0:21:12); PUB Order 27/18 (minutes R20-078).
mover: R19-063 Susan Penner; R20-074 and R20-078 Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: R19-063 Jac Siemens; R20-074, R20-078 Jac Siemens

title: 126 Maplewood apartment rezoning approved after neighbours raise ditch water and drainage
summary: A 56-signature petition opposed rezoning 126 Maplewood Street for a 9-unit apartment; one concern was more water in the ditching behind the lots, and a question was asked about Home Street drainage. Staff said development may not drain more or faster than before, and Michael Zwaagstra said the development agreement fixes how drainage is set up before construction.
status_detail: Second reading of rezoning By-law 2120 carried unanimously (R19-118).
figures: 9 units; petition with 56 signatures (transcript 0:10:02).
reasons: engineering-standard: Province and city rules require post-development drainage to be no greater or faster than before. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); not-grounds-to-block-development: Drainage is handled in the development agreement before third reading, so it is not a reason to refuse the rezoning. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: R.W. presented a 56-signature petition; one neighbour worried about water in the ditch increasing. The owner (R.B.) proposed closing the open ditch with a culvert.

title: 1-foot side-yard variance denied 5-1 because staff warned of drainage and overland flooding risk
summary: A homeowner in the new Lexington Village area asked to build a garage 1 foot from the side lot line instead of 4. Staff and the city engineer warned it could block the common swale and raise overland flooding risk for both houses. Michael Zwaagstra moved to deny, saying water is a major issue in Steinbach; Jac Siemens wanted a 2-foot variance but found no seconder.
status_detail: Siemens' motion for a 2-foot variance died for lack of a seconder; the denial carried 5-1 (R19-158), Jake Hiebert excused.
figures: 1-foot side yard requested vs 4-foot minimum; eaves may come no closer than 2 feet (transcript 0:05:06, 0:09:49).
reasons: engineering-standard: Staff and the city engineer flagged overland-flooding risk; ignoring them leaves the problem to a future council. (Michael Zwaagstra); extreme-storm: The last 5-inch rain event brought many complaints; untested new areas need caution. (Earl Funk)
public: A neighbour from another street (M.G.) said a similar encroachment sends her neighbours' water onto her lot and urged denial.

title: Mayor refers to a recent '5 inches over 2 days' rain event and many complaints
summary: While denying a side-yard variance in August 2019, Mayor Funk said the last water event, 5 inches of rain over 2 days, brought many emails and phone calls about water problems. No report on that event, its damage or the city's response came to an open council meeting in the transcripts searched.
status_detail: Mentioned only in passing; no public report, count of affected homes or follow-up found in 2019 transcripts or minutes.
figures: '5 inches over 2 days' (Mayor, transcript 2019-08-06 0:19:06); exact date of the event not stated.
notes: The published sewer-backups report says residents report Georgetown sewage backups in 2019; no council discussion of a 2019 Georgetown backup was found in the 2018-2022 transcripts. No transcripts exist for Oct 15 - Dec 17, 2019.

title: Site-width variance for an 8-plex at 44 First Street approved 5-2 over Siemens' drainage objection
summary: After rezoning 44 First Street for an 8-unit building (4-3 vote), council approved a variance reducing the required site width from 75 to 70 feet. Jac Siemens opposed, saying a neighbour-built drain behind the lot shows past water problems and more roof and parking surface could push water onto neighbours; Michael Zwaagstra replied that staff had not flagged drainage this time.
status_detail: Variance approved 5-2 (R19-170); the rezoning's third reading had carried 4-3 (R19-169) on other grounds.
figures: Site width 70 ft vs 75 ft required (transcript 0:12:02).
reasons: engineering-standard: Staff recommended approval and did not flag drainage, unlike the Alexander Way variance. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Federal-provincial infrastructure grants sought for three water and sewer renewals
summary: Council applied to the Investing in Canada Infrastructure Program (Green Infrastructure stream) for three projects on its long-term capital plan: Kroeker Avenue, Brandt Street and Loewen Boulevard water, wastewater and road reconstruction. Members stressed renewing old pipes at a fraction of the cost if grants came through.
status_detail: All three applications approved unanimously (R19-177 to R19-179). Kroeker Avenue (2020) and Brandt Street (2021) went ahead funded by local improvement borrowing and utility reserves; whether any ICIP grant was received was not confirmed in council records searched.
figures: Kroeker Ave $2,930,000 total; Brandt St $5,210,000; Loewen Blvd $2,815,000 (minutes R19-177/178/179). Brandt St: about 40% federal and about a third provincial if approved (transcript 0:10:39).
reasons: cost: Renewing infrastructure at about 30 cents on the dollar would be unwise to pass up. (Damian Penner (medium-confidence identification))
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner
seconder: Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert; Susan Penner

title: Kroeker Avenue rebuilt with new water and sewer mains
summary: Council used a local improvement plan to borrow for the reconstruction of three blocks of Kroeker Avenue, including the water main and sewer main, and awarded the tender below budget.
status_detail: LIP By-law 2131 first and second reading Dec 17, 2019 (R19-248, R19-249), third reading Mar 3, 2020 (R20-051); tender awarded (R20-052); debenture by-law 2167 followed in Dec 2020.
figures: Borrowing authority up to $2.21M (Municipal Board Order E-20-019, transcript 2020-03-03 0:54:37); tender $1,797,432 to Maple Leaf Construction (minutes R20-052).
reasons: already-doing: Administration flagged the street for rebuilding and it was time. (Damian Penner)
mover: R20-051 Damian Penner; R20-052 Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: R20-051 Jake Hiebert; R20-052 Bill Hiebert

title: Harmony Lane retention pond land dedicated by plan of works
summary: Council passed By-law 2149, a plan of works dedicating developer land in the Harmony Lane subdivision to the city for stormwater management (a retention pond). Damian Penner and Mayor Funk said a city as flat as Steinbach needs to control stormwater.
status_detail: First reading Apr 21 (R20-085), second and third reading May 5, 2020 (R20-098, R20-099), all unanimous.
reasons: engineering-standard: A city with the topography of a postage stamp needs stormwater management in place. (Damian Penner)
mover: Damian Penner; Susan Penner; Bill Hiebert
seconder: Susan Penner; Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert

title: Maplewood multifamily rezoning approved after a Home Street North resident raises runoff
summary: During the hearing on By-law 2147 (rezoning 135-191 Maplewood Street for multifamily buildings), a Home Street North resident described ongoing drainage problems on his street and asked that new development reduce runoff, noting green space would shrink sharply. Staff repeated the rule that outflow must not exceed pre-development levels; the mayor said he shared the drainage concern but council must trust the engineers.
status_detail: Second reading carried (transcript). No minutes for May 19, 2020 are on file, so the resolution number and vote record are unavailable.
reasons: engineering-standard: Stormwater leaving a redeveloped site must not exceed the pre-development rate. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); engineering-standard: Engineers on both sides should be trusted to design drainage. (Earl Funk)
public: K.B. (Home Street North) said drainage issues on his street are 'dear to my heart' and estimated a 60-70% loss of green space on the site; the applicant (J.P.) said the drainage plan was not yet designed but all water must be held on site.

title: Ellis Avenue 6-plex rezoning denied; Siemens says lot fixes can push water onto neighbours
summary: Neighbours opposing a 6-unit rezoning at 14 Ellis Avenue said the low lot floods every year and asked where the water would go. Staff said a drainage plan is standard and water must drain to the street. Council denied second reading, mainly on neighbourhood-fit and infill-policy grounds; Jac Siemens added that development agreements fix water on one lot but can push it onto others, while the city 'washes its hands' because it is private property.
status_detail: Second reading of By-law 2152 denied unanimously (R20-156). A revised 14 Ellis Avenue application (By-law 2190) returned in Oct 2021.
reasons: private-property: Standing water moved off one lot becomes a neighbour's problem and the city largely stays out because it is private property. (Jac Siemens)
public: B.T. (Ellis Avenue) said the property is low, its owner pumps water every year, and asked where the water would go.
notes: Drainage was a secondary reason; the stated grounds for denial were density, setbacks and the infill policy.

title: First Street rezoning refused at first reading after the city engineer warned drainage would worsen
summary: Staff recommended denying first reading of By-law 2165 (24 units at 85 and part of 79 First Street); the city engineer's report said redevelopment would worsen existing drainage problems on 79 First Street. Michael Zwaagstra moved denial citing poor lot configuration, the engineer's drainage warning and the infill policy. Damian Penner opposed, wanting the drainage questions answered at a public hearing.
status_detail: Motion to deny first reading carried (transcript). No minutes for Nov 17, 2020 are on file, so the recorded vote is unknown.
reasons: engineering-standard: The city engineer explicitly said the redevelopment would worsen drainage on the neighbouring lot. (Michael Zwaagstra)
vote: not recorded (carried; at least Damian Penner and a second Councillor Penner said they would vote against)
notes: Drainage was one of several reasons (lot configuration, infill policy, expected objections).

title: Brandt Street water main replaced and sewer main relined (about 1 km)
summary: Council approved a local improvement plan to replace the Brandt Street water main and reline the sewer main between First Street and McKenzie Avenue using trenchless lining technology, then awarded the tender even though bids came in over budget, dropping a sidewalk and adding $300,000 from the utility reserve.
status_detail: LIP By-law 2160 first/second reading Dec 15, 2020 (R20-252, R20-253), third reading Mar 16, 2021 (R21-057); tender awarded Apr 6, 2021 (R21-065); debenture By-law 2194 passed Dec 21, 2021 and Feb 15, 2022 (R21-274, R21-275, R22-045). The minutes describe the work as completed.
figures: Estimated $2.415M, of which $1.25M borrowed (transcript 2020-12-15 0:34:38); tender $2,342,325 to Maple Leaf Construction plus $300,000 from the utility reserve, budget $2.715M (transcript 2021-04-06 0:38:13; minutes R21-065).
reasons: cost: Doing underground work on time and with new lining technology costs far less than waiting. (Susan Penner); already-doing: Older established areas need renewal, not just new development. (Michael Zwaagstra)
seconder: R20-252 Susan Penner; R21-057 Jac Siemens; R21-065 Susan Penner

title: After-the-fact 1.9-foot side-yard variance denied 6-1 over drainage and fire risk
summary: An owner built a house addition 1.9 feet from the lot line under a permit for a detached shed. Staff said it would likely cause drainage problems and was a fire hazard. Council denied the variance, meaning the structure must be made to comply; Jac Siemens preferred approving it with a substantial fine.
figures: 1.9-foot east side yard vs 4-foot minimum (minutes R21-063).
reasons: engineering-standard: Staff said it would cause drainage problems; a fine would fix nothing. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The neighbour objected in writing (correspondence on file).

title: Harmony Lane Phase 11: neighbours' concrete-swale request not made a condition; new storm pond created
summary: Neighbours on Hespeler Street South wrote asking that a concrete-bottom swale be required for the 37-lot Harmony Lane Phase 11. Staff said the swale in the previous phase was developer-initiated, not a city requirement; council approved the rezoning without adding it. In 2022 council passed a plan of works creating a stormwater-management parcel for the phase.
status_detail: Rezoning By-law 2189 passed (R21-217, R21-218) with no swale condition; the developer said it would follow city and engineer requirements. Plan of works By-law 2201 for the stormwater parcel passed first/second reading Apr 5 (R22-088, R22-089) and third reading Apr 19, 2022 (R22-099).
reasons: engineering-standard: A concrete swale was not a city requirement; the earlier one was the developer's choice. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: K.B. and G.B. (Hespeler Street South) wrote with drainage concerns and asked that a concrete-bottom swale be required. The applicant's representative (D.B.) said the developer would comply with whatever city and project engineers require.
mover: R21-217 Michael Zwaagstra; R21-218 Susan Penner; R22-099 Damian Penner
seconder: R21-217 Susan Penner; R21-218 Jake Hiebert; R22-099 Bill Hiebert

title: 2022 capital program: Loewen Boulevard sewer extension, Brookdale Crescent sewer and water, Loewen/PTH 12 land drainage sewer
summary: The 2022 budget listed a Loewen Boulevard sewer extension (new capital) and Brookdale Crescent sewer and water replacement (renewal), and the Loewen Boulevard/PTH 12 intersection local improvement included the sewer main and a land drainage sewer. Council awarded the bundled 2022 capital works tender, which Michael Zwaagstra called an aggressive capital works plan.
status_detail: Loewen/PTH 12 LIP By-law 2187: first and second reading Dec 7, 2021 (R21-250, R21-251), third reading Mar 15, 2022 (R22-067). 2022 capital works tender awarded Mar 1, 2022 (R22-053). 2022 financial plan adopted Apr 5, 2022 (moved Zwaagstra, seconded Siemens). In Sept 2022 the developer's representative said the city had improved the sewer line along Loewen Boulevard from Walnut Street to Old Tom Road (minutes 2022-09-06).
figures: 2022 capital works tender $2,083,853 to Maple Leaf Construction (minutes R22-053); 2022 budget $25.3M new capital and $13.9M renewal (minutes 2022-04-05).
reasons: already-doing: Basic infrastructure remains a priority; the capital plan is aggressive. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: R21-250 Jac Siemens; R21-251, R22-053, R22-067 Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: R21-250 Damian Penner; R21-251, R22-053 Bill Hiebert; R22-067 Susan Penner
notes: The Apr 5, 2022 financial-plan meeting video has no audio; budget items come from the minutes.

title: Lexington Village final phase approved with partial closure of a temporary drain; Jake Hiebert raises Bush Farm Road culvert
summary: Council approved the 62-lot final phase of Lexington Village subject to a later by-law partly closing an existing drain. Jake Hiebert asked about water flowing in from the south and noted a past problem with the culvert under Bush Farm Road; the developer said the existing retention pond was oversized for the whole development and rules bar releasing more water than the field did.
status_detail: Subdivision approved unanimously (R22-033). No follow-up on the Bush Farm Road culvert was found in 2022 records.
figures: 62 lots (transcript 0:06:37).
reasons: engineering-standard: Pond sized for the whole development; outflow limited to pre-development levels. (developer representative D.B.)
public: The applicant's representative (D.B.) said: 'we cannot drain any more water than originally came in'.

title: Park Hill Phase 2 sewage lift station site approved, paid by the developer
summary: Council passed By-law 2146, a plan of works creating a lot for a sewage lift station in the Park Hill Phase 2 development north of McKenzie Avenue, part of the approved servicing plan. Staff confirmed the developer pays for it under the development agreement.
status_detail: First reading Apr 19 (R22-101), second and third reading Jun 21, 2022 (R22-156, R22-157), all unanimous.
reasons: already-doing: A lift station is part of the cost of development and the phase is needed for lot supply. (Susan Penner)
mover: Susan Penner; Jac Siemens; Damian Penner
seconder: Damian Penner; Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert

title: City applies for Disaster Financial Assistance after April-May 2022 rain and overland flooding
summary: After the province declared the spring 2022 flooding a DFA event, council passed the resolution needed for Steinbach homeowners to apply for Disaster Financial Assistance for flood losses not covered by insurance, such as water through basement windows. The city manager said administration had not known of significant damage until residents raised it, and estimated 5 to 10 potential claims.
status_detail: Resolution R22-198 carried unanimously on Aug 16, 2022, about three months after the flooding. The number of approved claims was not reported in 2022 records.
figures: 5 to 10 potential claims in Steinbach (transcript 0:32:21); maximum federal contribution $84,000 cited by a councillor (transcript 0:31:55).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: The provincial DFA program, not the city, pays uninsured overland-flood losses; the city's role is to pass a resolution and file the application. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: Damian Penner credited 'advocates within the community' who told administration about the damage.

title: Neighbours' flooding objections to the 128-acre Old Tom Road/Loewen Boulevard development; council approves on engineers' assurances
themes: development; overland-flooding; drainage; lift-station; residents; independent-study
summary: Neighbours of a multi-phase development east of Hespeler (Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard) said the low corner and creek already flood in spring and heavy rain, asked for a retention pond and an overall impact study including surface runoff, and one raised sewer backup problems west of Hespeler. The developer said the waterway would be built first with three flow restrictors, a developer-paid lift station would serve the area, and a drainage report met the city's higher-than-provincial standard. Council approved all four items unanimously; several members said engineering would improve drainage.
status_detail: OCP amendment, two rezonings and the 95-lot subdivision approved unanimously (R22-201 to R22-205). The requested retention pond on the corner and an independent overall impact study were not required; drainage was left to the development agreement and engineering report.
figures: 128 acres; 95 parcels in phase 1 (transcript 1:23:35); lift station $1.2-1.4M paid by developer (developer representative, transcript 1:05:38); three flow restrictors (transcript 0:41:02); about 2 inches of rain recently (resident, transcript 0:14:38).
reasons: not-grounds-to-block-development: Months of engineering by the city, the developer's engineers and the province must be accepted. (Michael Zwaagstra); engineering-standard: Engineered drainage canals in his own area improved water flow. (Damian Penner); engineering-standard: As watershed chair he has faith in engineers and expects drainage to improve. (Jake Hiebert (medium-confidence identification)); private-property: Recent backyard drainage problems were caused by residents over-landscaping, not by bad engineering. (Earl Funk)
public: R.F. (Loewen Boulevard) said he had raised flooding on his yard for years, the creek and its buffer were not shown, and asked for a retention pond, a surface-water runoff plan and an overall impact study; he also cited 'sewer backup problems in the area west of Hespeler'. K.C. and L.C. said the waterway through their property floods quickly and feared backing up. J.C. said his property is close to flood levels in large rainfalls. Developer representative W.N. said the waterway would be built first and the city requires exceeding the provincial standard. These are residents' claims, not findings.
mover: R22-201 Michael Zwaagstra; R22-202 Jac Siemens; R22-203 Susan Penner; R22-205 Damian Penner
seconder: R22-201 Susan Penner; R22-202 Damian Penner; R22-203 Michael Zwaagstra; R22-205 Jac Siemens
notes: The resident's 'sewer backup problems in the area west of Hespeler' were not answered by council; the developer's representative said the new lift station 'should not affect anybody's sewer backup anywhere else'. At 0:45:51 a councillor (voice D = Siemens, but preceded by a hand-off to Damian Penner) asked how water would get over the hill; attribution conflicted, so not quoted.

title: New water and wastewater rate plan (By-law 2163) given first reading
summary: With the 2018 rate plan expired at the end of 2020, council gave first reading to a new water and wastewater rate by-law with increases of about 3-4% a year for 2023-2026, to go to the Public Utilities Board for review.
status_detail: First reading Sept 6, 2022 (R22-209, unanimous); no further readings found by Dec 2022 (PUB review pending).
figures: About $1 to $1.35 per month more for a typical residential customer each year 2023-2026 (transcript 1:33:25); about 3-4% a year (transcript 1:34:46).
reasons: cost: PUB rules require rates close to the actual cost of service. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: McKenzie Avenue fourplex rezoning approved 5-2; Damian Penner says redevelopment usually improves neighbours' drainage
summary: Neighbours with 22 letters of objection opposed rezoning a lot near McKenzie Avenue and Cottonwood for a fourplex, one asking about elevation and drainage. Damian Penner said redeveloped lots must submit an approved lot-drainage plan and usually improve drainage for the properties around them.
status_detail: Second reading of By-law 2217 carried 5-2 (R22-253); the votes against cited traffic and neighbourhood fit, not drainage.
reasons: engineering-standard: Lot-drainage plans required on redevelopment keep water on site and often improve neighbours' drainage. (Damian Penner)
public: C.K. presented 22 letters of objection (traffic, privacy, property values) and asked about buffering and elevation (drainage).

title: Elmdale Street drain formalized by a plan-of-drain by-law
summary: By-law 2197 registered a plan of drain for the public drain along Elmdale Street between Barkman and Reimer avenues, as part of consolidating land for the events centre. Members said nothing about the drain's function would change.
status_detail: First and second reading Jan 3, 2023 (R23-004, R23-005); third reading Jan 17, 2023 (R23-018).

title: Lift Station 2 on Loewen Boulevard upgraded and expanded ($2M borrowed)
summary: Council held a local-improvement hearing and borrowed $2M (By-law 2221) to upgrade three pumps, expand Lift Station 2 at 330 Loewen Boulevard and add a sewer force main. Members justified it mainly as added capacity so east-side subdivisions could proceed, and as renewal of one of the city's oldest lift stations. When the tender came in over the engineer's estimate, council topped it up from the utility reserve and later issued the debenture.
status_detail: By-law 2221 first/second reading Jan 3, 2023 (R23-008/009), third reading Mar 21, 2023 after Municipal Board approval (R23-054); construction tender awarded Oct 17, 2023 (R23-213); debenture By-law 2239 given third reading Mar 5, 2024 (R24-055). Siemens said in Mar 2024 it should be finished that year.
figures: Estimated $2.265M, $2M borrowed over 5 years at max 8% (transcript Jan 3, 2023, 0:11:29 and 0:12:00); engineer's estimate just under $1.7M vs low bid $1,996,642.57 plus $250,000 from the utility reserve (R23-213; transcript Oct 17, 2023, 0:22:35, 0:24:13); TD Bank debenture 5.41% for 5 years (transcript Mar 5, 2024, 0:47:38). Siemens: part of 'about an $8 million project in total' (Oct 17, 2023, 0:25:15).
reasons: growth-capacity: Subdivisions on the east end of Loewen Boulevard could not develop without more sewer capacity. (Jac Siemens); already-doing: Basic infrastructure is the top priority; continued sewer upgrades are money well spent. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: No one spoke at the Jan 3, 2023 local-improvement hearing and there was no written correspondence (transcript 0:12:23).
notes: The 'about $8 million' total is Siemens's estimate; the components were not itemized on the record.

title: 2023 and 2024 financial plans: steady underground renewal, but some renewal projects pushed back
summary: Both budgets kept underground infrastructure renewal as a stated priority and included the Lift Station 2 upgrade. In 2024, the toughest budget members could recall (5.1% mill-rate rise, driven by construction inflation and the events centre), Siemens said some renewal projects were spread into later years. Before the storm he described Steinbach as having fewer infrastructure problems than other communities.
status_detail: 2023 plan adopted Mar 21, 2023 (R23-053); 2024 plan adopted Apr 2, 2024 (R24-073).
figures: 2023: capital program $67.3M, almost $4M for underground renewal (transcript Mar 21, 2023, 0:08:50, 0:23:35); water and wastewater utility operating cost $4.2M. 2024: capital $62.7M, mill rate 14.4 (+~5%), utility rates +4%, utility operating cost $4.5M (transcript Apr 2, 2024, 0:05:52, 0:08:30); $16.5M to infrastructure renewal (D. Penner, 0:26:08, speaker medium).
reasons: cost: Inflation and the events centre forced some renewal projects into later years. (Jac Siemens); already-doing: Steady renewal means fewer infrastructure problems than in other communities. (Jac Siemens)
public: No public comments at either financial plan hearing.
notes: The 2024 budget presenter's turns are mislabelled as a councillor in the speaker map, so figures from that presentation are cited by timestamp, not quoted.

title: Loewen Boulevard force main deferred to 2024 to cover cost overruns, then built with a reduced scope
summary: In March 2023 a road and sewer renewal tender (Barkman Avenue) came in about $690,000 over budget; council covered it partly by postponing the force main components of the Lift Station 2 project to 2024. In March 2024 the Loewen Boulevard force main drew a single bid above budget; staff negotiated a reduced scope and council awarded it.
status_detail: Force main work deferred one year (R23-058, Mar 21, 2023), then awarded with a reduced scope to Accurate HD Ltd. for $491,693 (R24-065, Mar 19, 2024). What was cut from the scope was not stated on the record.
figures: Barkman tender overage about $690,000; LS2 scope revision freed $265,000 from the utility operating fund (transcript Mar 21, 2023, 0:53:49, 0:57:01). 2024 force main: single bid $570,310, awarded at $491,693 plus taxes (transcript Mar 19, 2024, 2:19:08; R24-065).
reasons: cost: Tenders were coming in well over budget because of construction inflation; projects were reshuffled to stay within approved funds. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Lift Station 1 upgrade and lagoon force main twinning: planned in 2023, design hired in Nov 2024
summary: The 2023 financial plan already listed 'the twinning of a force main' in the 2024 capital program. In June 2024 council asked the Manitoba Water Services Board to pay half the design costs of twinning the force main from Lift Station 1 to the lagoon. After the September storm, council hired Associated Engineering to design the Lift Station 1 upgrades and the twinning, correcting the award amount two weeks later.
status_detail: Water Services Board request Jun 18, 2024 (R24-127); engineering award Nov 5, 2024 (R24-209, $529,789.89) corrected to $463,201 on Nov 19, 2024 (R24-223). Construction came later (see the 2025-2026 record: Lift Station 1 tender awarded Mar 17, 2026).
figures: 2024 capital program then budgeted at $36.1M including the force main twinning (transcript Mar 21, 2023, 0:18:59); WSB asked for 50% of design costs (R24-127); engineering $463,201 plus taxes, five proposals received, RFP closed Oct 23, 2024 (R24-223; Nov 5 minutes 12.1).
reasons: cost: Apply for provincial funding streams or lose access to them. (Damian Penner)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (R24-127); Jac Siemens (R24-209); Damian Penner (R24-223)
notes: Whether the RFP was issued before or after the Sept 2024 storm was not stated; it closed Oct 23, 2024.

title: Council supports expanding the Seine Rat Roseau Watershed District
summary: Council endorsed the province's proposal to expand the Seine Rat Roseau Watershed District (adding the RM of Morris), moved by its council representative Jake Hiebert. Earlier that year the mayor credited Councillor Hiebert's work on the watershed board for a water detention project at the museum that addressed drainage concerns.
status_detail: Approved Aug 15, 2023 (R23-173). Jake Hiebert was re-appointed watershed representative on Nov 7, 2023 (organizational minutes). Watershed minutes were received as information at most meetings.
notes: The mayor's 'Councillor Hebert' is taken to be Jake Hiebert because he is the watershed representative; the project's date and cost were not stated.

title: Manning Canal drain designated for a new subdivision near Loewen Boulevard and Old Tom Road
summary: By-law 2228 opened a drain plan for part of the Manning Canal drain north of Loewen Boulevard and Old Tom Road, as part of a residential development. The mayor said it would fix drainage problems at that corner.
status_detail: First and second reading Jun 20, 2023 (R23-127, R23-128). No third reading was found in the parsed minutes through 2026.
notes: The mover's comment at 0:37:13 (minutes: Damian Penner moved) is labelled as a public speaker in the speaker map, so it is not quoted. Third reading may have followed outside the parsed minutes; unverified.

title: Developments approved on condition that owners manage their own runoff
summary: Across subdivision and variance hearings, council required updated drainage or lot-grading plans approved by the city engineer and told owners they must manage water on their own sites. In Sept 2024, the same day as the storm report, council approved a large garage in an older neighbourhood only with a lot-grading plan, because those lots were built before lot-grading rules.
status_detail: Examples: Jul 18, 2023 subdivision subject to an updated drainage plan; Aug 1, 2023 rezoning (By-law 2230) where the developer described a land drainage system and water retention area (minutes); Mar 5, 2024 Variance V-2024-01 subject to a lot grading and servicing plan; Sep 17, 2024 Variance V-2024-12 approved subject to a lot grading plan (R24-180).
reasons: private-property: Owners are responsible for drainage on their own sites. (Jac Siemens); engineering-standard: An updated drainage plan is standard for all developments and subdivisions. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: At the Nov 5, 2024 hearing on rezoning By-law 2253 (minutes only; no transcript), G.W., a neighbour, cited existing drainage issues and asked how water would be managed; the developer said drainage could improve with the flat roof. Second reading carried (R24-207).
notes: Grouped: several routine hearings with the same condition.

title: Unbuilt lane off First Street closed and kept as a public drain (5-2)
summary: By-law 2232 closed a registered but never-built public lane behind First Street lots next to PTH 52 and converted it to a plan of works, because the strip has always carried a major public drain. A neighbouring landowner objected in writing, wanting a back lane for development. Staff said putting a road over the drain would be very costly, and the mayor said the area would be prone to flooding.
status_detail: First reading Oct 3, 2023 (R23-198); second and third readings Nov 7, 2023 (R23-226, R23-227), 5-2. It fulfilled a condition of an earlier subdivision approval.
reasons: cost: Keeping the drain working with a road over it would be extremely costly. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); engineering-standard: Steinbach is flat and needs every drain; covering it would leave the neighbourhood prone to flooding. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: One written objection from a neighbouring landowner/developer who owns several First Street lots and wanted rear-lane access (name not used; initials not confirmed). Staff said every affected lot has street access.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (second reading); Bill Hiebert (third reading)
notes: The mayor's transcribed 'Stammack' is Steinbach.

title: Development and water-and-sewer impact fees raised 5% a year, not the 7.5% staff recommended
summary: By-law 2233 merged the residential and non-residential capital development fees and the water and sewer impact fee, which fund growth-related capacity such as lagoon expansion and future mechanical wastewater treatment. Staff recommended 7.5% yearly increases for four years; Zwaagstra moved 5% to match construction inflation and protect affordability. Damian Penner and Jake Hiebert voted against at every reading, arguing growth should pay its own way rather than the mill rate.
status_detail: Adopted at 5% a year for 2024-2027 (R23-211, R23-224, R23-225), half-way between the old 2.5% and staff's 7.5%; members said it would be reviewed in 2027.
figures: Fees had risen 2.5% a year since 2012 while construction costs rose about 5-6% (Zwaagstra, transcript Oct 17, 2023, 0:08:47); SPC options were 2.5%, 5%, 7.5% and 10%, with about 11% over four years needed to catch up (D. Penner, Nov 7, 2023, 0:06:44).
reasons: housing-affordability: Fees are passed on to home buyers; 5% matches construction inflation and errs on the side of affordability. (Michael Zwaagstra); housing-affordability: Entry-level housing would be hit hardest by 7.5%; other governments are pushing affordability. (Mayor Earl Funk); growth-pays: (against) Fees have not covered growth costs since 2012, shifting them onto the mill rate. (Damian Penner); growth-pays: (against) The city pays the difference from taxpayers, which is unfair. (Jake Hiebert)
seconder: Jac Siemens (first); Bill Hiebert (second); Susan Penner (third)
vote: 5-2 at each reading (against: Damian Penner, Jake Hiebert)
notes: Fees fund growth capacity generally; the debate did not mention basement backups.

title: Setback variance on PTH 52 West denied partly over drainage
summary: Administration recommended denying a request to cut a side-yard setback from 15 feet to 4 feet for an accessory building on a 4-acre lot on PTH 52 West, citing future drainage limitations for neighbouring land. Council denied it; Bill Hiebert was the lone vote against denial.
status_detail: Variance V-2023-22 denied (R23-251), 5-1; Damian Penner was excused.
reasons: drainage-protection: Setbacks exist partly for drainage; no drainage plan was submitted and undeveloped neighbouring land could be harmed later. (Jake Hiebert); fairness-precedent: Approving would set a precedent for rural parcels likely to develop. (Jac Siemens)
public: The applicant did not attend; no objections were raised.

title: Residents' standing-water complaints (Chrysler Gate, Harmony Lane): no city work needed, report received
summary: After a wet, cool spring, residents G.P. and P.P. of Chrysler Gate wrote to council about standing water; L.R. and J.R. of Harmony Lane raised a similar concern. Council referred the letter to administration. The engineering department found the city's drainage swales were built to the approved plans and within tolerances, suggested one owner make minor changes on their own lot, and expected the problem to resolve as the ground dried. Council accepted the report as information.
status_detail: Referred to administration by consensus May 21, 2024; report received as information Jul 16, 2024 with no remedial work on the city swales.
reasons: engineering-standard: Swales were built to the approved plans and verified elevations were within the city's tolerances. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); private-property: The city engineer suggested an owner make minor surface changes on their own lot. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); unusual-weather: Excessive spring rainfall and cool temperatures caused abnormal standing water; drier weather was expected to resolve it. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: G.P. and P.P. (letter, May 10, 2024) and L.R. and J.R. (letter) reported standing water and drainage problems behind their homes.
notes: Residents identified by initials only. The transcript says '2014 Chrysler Gate'; the minutes give the address as 214.

title: September 16-17, 2024 storm: same-day report to council on overland flooding and sewer flows
summary: The day after about 6 inches of rain fell, the city manager reported that ditches, creeks and drainage channels were at or over capacity, the stormwater flood pump at the main Park Road West lift station had run since 9 a.m., all lift stations were pumping at full capacity, roads were overtopped and washed out, and the T.G. Smith Centre flooded. Staff would assess how many homes had overland flooding or sewer backups. No council member asked a question. On Nov 5, 2024 (minutes only; no transcript) staff reported that several dozen property owners had reported basement flooding and that the city had shared information on the province's storm damage recovery program.
status_detail: Follow-up given Nov 5, 2024: 'several dozen' owners reported basement flooding directly to the city (minutes item 11.2); no full count of affected homes, cause analysis or homeowner program was presented in 2024. No other recorded council discussion of the backups was found in Oct-Dec 2024 transcripts.
figures: About 6 inches of rain (media reports), more than 3 inches on the morning of Sept 17 (Nov 5 minutes); flood pump capacity 485 litres per second; 16 road washouts (transcript Sep 17, 2024, 0:26:13, 0:28:12).
reasons: extreme-storm: Saturated ground plus an exceptional amount of rain overwhelmed open drainage. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
notes: The Nov 5, 2024 meeting has minutes but no transcript in the project, so the update and any discussion could not be quoted. One sentence break in the 0:26:13 quote ('operation. Until') is as transcribed.

title: Council asks the province for Disaster Financial Assistance for the September 2024 storm
summary: On Nov 5, 2024 council passed a resolution requesting funding under Manitoba's Disaster Financial Assistance program for the Sept 16-17 rain event. Staff said the city had been in contact with the Manitoba Emergency Measures Organization and had shared information on the EMO storm damage recovery program, which may be available to affected property owners.
status_detail: Request made (R24-214); no response was reported to council by Dec 31, 2024. The province's response is covered in the 2025-2026 record.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Relief for property owners pointed to the provincial DFA / EMO program rather than a city program. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
notes: Minutes only; the Nov 5, 2024 meeting has no transcript in the project, so no quotes or debate are available.

title: Council applies for federal funding for a climate risk assessment and adaptation plan
summary: On Dec 3, 2024 council resolved to apply to the FCM Green Municipal Fund's Local Leadership for Climate Adaptation initiative, which would pay 70% of hiring consultants to prepare a climate risk assessment and adaptation plan. Members framed it as worthwhile if appropriate and useful for future grant applications; the September storm was not mentioned.
status_detail: Application approved (R24-242). The resulting climate risk assessment was presented to council in August 2026 (see the 2025-2026 record).
figures: FCM would fund 70% of project costs (transcript Dec 3, 2024, 0:50:52).
reasons: study-first: A study could help when applying for future grants from other governments. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Draft new community plan: new development must not add runoff beyond pre-development levels
summary: Presenting the Official Community Plan and zoning review on Dec 3, 2024, Damian Penner highlighted a policy, already applied in practice and raised often at public hearings, that new developments must control runoff so their contribution to the land drainage system is no greater than before development. Council accepted the recommended amendments and told staff to prepare the documents for public engagement and adoption in 2025.
status_detail: R24-234 accepted the recommendations and authorized drafting; public engagement planned for mid-January 2025, readings and hearings Feb-Mar 2025 (minutes item 7.4). Adoption falls outside this period.
reasons: already-doing: The runoff rule writes down what the city already does in principle. (Damian Penner)
notes: The minutes summary of the OCP changes does not list the runoff policy; it is sourced from the transcript.

title: Lift Station 1 to lagoon force main twinning approved ($6.6M), with a provincial grant request
summary: Council held the public hearing on Local Improvement Plan 2025-01 (By-law 2255) to lay about 3 km of new force main along Park Road West from Lift Station 1 to the lagoon, and upgrade the lift station. No one objected. Council framed it as growth capacity: Susan Penner noted towns whose growth stalled when sewer capacity ran out. On Feb 18 council asked the Manitoba Water Services Board (MWSB) for 50% of the cost, and gave third reading on Jul 2, 2025 after Municipal Board approval.
status_detail: First and second reading Feb 4, 2025 (R25-025, R25-026); MWSB grant request Feb 18 (R25-038); third reading Jul 2, 2025 (R25-137). The force main contract was awarded Feb 17, 2026 (see 2026-force-main-tender).
figures: Project $6.595M; borrowing up to $2.75M over 5 years at max 7%; about 0.488 mills, just under $50/yr for a $250,000 home (transcript Feb 4, 2025, 0:05:25). MWSB request: 50% of construction (R25-038).
public: No objections at the public hearing.
mover: Susan Penner (1st), Jac Siemens (2nd, MWSB), Michael Zwaagstra (3rd)
seconder: Jac Siemens (1st), Bill Hiebert (2nd), Jake Hiebert (MWSB), Susan Penner (3rd)

title: Province says no disaster aid for the September 2024 storm
summary: On Feb 18, 2025 council received a letter from Manitoba's Emergency Management Organization saying Steinbach did not qualify for Disaster Financial Assistance (DFA) for the September 2024 rainstorm. Jac Siemens asked whether there was an appeal and whether homeowners were denied too. The City Manager said the city's own damages were well below the DFA threshold, that the city's application is what opens the program to private owners, and that he knew of no appeal process.
status_detail: Received as information (minutes item 21); no appeal was pursued at the time. Council later asked the province to reopen this file together with the 2025 one (see 2026-dfa-reopen-request).
figures: No dollar figures given; Warkentin: city's own damages 'significantly below the general threshold' (transcript 1:01:17).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: DFA is a provincial program; owners apply directly and the province decides; no known appeal. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
notes: The transcript has the mayor reading the storm date as 'September 16th, 2017' (mis-transcription or misreading); the minutes only say correspondence from EMO was acknowledged. Context (2024 storm, DFA application) indicates the September 16-17, 2024 storm.

title: Climate risk assessment and adaptation plan: funded in 2025, promised for spring 2026
summary: Council funded a climate risk assessment in the 2025 budget and received a Green Municipal Fund grant of up to $70,000 for it (Jul 2, 2025). After the September 2025 storm the mayor called it the 'roadmap' for drainage projects, due in spring 2026. In March 2026 the City Manager said he expected it to be public.
status_detail: Not presented by spring 2026. According to the existing report (citing SteinbachOnline) it was presented on Aug 18, 2026 as a roadmap and was not adopted; that meeting has no transcript in this collection, so this is unverified here.
figures: FCM Green Municipal Fund grant up to $70,000 (minutes Jul 2, 2025, item 16).
reasons: study-first: Projects to be chosen once the climate plan gives a roadmap. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: M.R. asked on Mar 17, 2026 whether residents could see the results of the climate risk assessment.
notes: Aug 18, 2026 meeting not transcribed; status after that taken from the existing report.

title: 2025 budget lists the force main twinning and Millwork Drive sewer replacement
summary: The 2025 financial plan (capital program about $36.6M) named the Park Road West force main twinning and the Millwork Drive sewer replacement among its larger projects, and funded a climate risk assessment. These were the projects the city later pointed to after the September 2025 storm.
status_detail: Adopted unanimously (R25-048). Both sewer projects were tendered in early 2026 rather than built in 2025.
figures: Capital program $36.6M; water/wastewater utility operating cost $4.7M (transcript Mar 4, 2025, 0:07-0:11).
notes: Climate risk assessment funding is stated in the City Manager's Sept 16, 2025 report and Mar 17, 2026 presentation.

title: Council seeks federal help for a $132M wastewater plant, second force main and lift station upgrade
summary: Council ratified an application to the Canada Housing Infrastructure Fund for 50% of a $132.5M project: wastewater treatment upgrades, primary lift station building upgrades and a second force main. The City Manager explained the city chose to build its own plant rather than join the RSR Wastewater Co-op. This is about long-term capacity, not storm backups directly.
status_detail: Application ratified (R25-081). No funding decision was reported in later meetings; the mayor still called it 'the big wastewater project' to come on Mar 3, 2026.
figures: Eligible cost $132,475,000; city share $65,447,500 (R25-081); treatment plant component about $94M, force main/lift station about $8M (transcript 0:15:25).

title: Council commits to act after Susan Penner's own basement floods a second time
summary: Susan Penner, whose Georgetown basement flooded in 2024 and 2025, used her opening to say the city must act 'now', even moving other projects, and named streets used as retention ponds and sump pumps draining into the sewer. The mayor committed council to 'leave no stone unturned', to the climate plan, and to the projects with the biggest impact.
status_detail: Followed by a November 2025 study session (not recorded), a flood mitigation plan in the 2026 budget, the Clear Spring Greens reroute and the Land Drainage By-law. Most capital work was already planned before the storms; no root-cause study, homeowner subsidy or compensation followed.
notes: The video starts partway into Susan Penner's opening (transcript turn at 0:00:00).

title: City Manager's report on the Sept 11-12, 2025 storm: beyond a 1-in-100-year event
summary: Added to the agenda on Sept 16, 2025, the report said about 126 mm fell in 4 hours; drains, ditches and the sewer system ran at capacity; Lift Station 1's storm pump peaked at 465 L/s against a 434 L/s rating; several dozen owners reported water in basements. It listed possible causes on private property, said the storm exceeded a 1-in-100-year event 'far beyond the reasonable planning level for underground pipes', pointed to 2021-2023 sewer modelling and the planned 2026 projects, and said the city was working with Manitoba EMO on DFA. Residents attended but could not speak; the mayor invited a delegation.
status_detail: Report read into the record and published on the city website (mayor, 0:51:12). Agenda amended to add it (R25-175).
figures: 126 mm in 4 hours (up to 135 mm); storm pump on 12:12 a.m., max 465 L/s at 3:20 a.m. vs 434 L/s rated, off at 7:54 p.m.; 2024 storm 95.9 mm; July 4, 2002 storm 132.8 mm (transcript 0:41:04; minutes items 15-16).
reasons: extreme-storm: Storm exceeded a 1-in-100-year event, beyond what underground pipes are designed for. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); private-property: Basement water may come from windows, floor drains, failed backup devices or sump pumps. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); already-doing: Sewer modelling 2021-2023 and planned 2026 projects (Millwork Drive, Park Road West). (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: Residents who had flooded attended; the mayor said they could not speak that night and invited one spokesperson to come as a delegation.

title: City takes ownership of drains in new subdivisions (plans of works)
summary: Council passed plan-of-works by-laws and a subdivision so drains run through new developments stay with the city and are maintained: By-law 2267 (drain south of the Acres Drive/August Cove industrial lots, Oct-Nov 2025) and Subdivision 4451-2026-9241 at 60 McKenzie Avenue (drain parcel to the city, Jun 2, 2026). Councillors said city control means the drains will be kept up.
status_detail: By-law 2267 readings R25-190, R25-213, R25-214; Subdivision approved R26-113 subject to a plan-of-works by-law.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner; Jake Hiebert
seconder: Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert

title: Council backs a call for more provincial water and sewer funding
summary: Council supported a Manitoba Municipal Administrators' Association resolution urging the province to put more money into the Manitoba Water Services Board, which was oversubscribed. Zwaagstra tied it to lift stations; the mayor said water and wastewater are the most crucial thing for development.
status_detail: Resolution carried (R25-193). Outcome of the advocacy not reported.
figures: Mayor: MWSB funds only about $48M of projects a year; 103 municipalities' projects went unfunded (transcript 0:28:55).

title: Animal rescue flooded twice: asks the city to clear and reassess the creek near Keating Road
summary: M.N., president of Steinbach & Area Animal Rescue (39 Keating Road), said the non-profit's building flooded in 2024 and 2025 and was told both times it was a 1-in-100-year flood. She asked for three things: immediate clearing of the creek beside the property, a formal engineering reassessment of the creek and outlet, and a regular maintenance schedule. The mayor said it would go into the stormwater drainage investigation for council's study session.
status_detail: On Mar 17, 2026 the City Manager reported a Keating Drain cleanout from PTH 52 West north to Park Road West, about $30,000, completed by November 2025; this appears to answer the first request. No engineering reassessment or maintenance schedule for that channel was reported.
figures: Insurance deductible $25,000 (delegation); Keating Drain cleanout about $30,000 (transcript Mar 17, 2026, 0:17:48).
reasons: extreme-storm: She said the city told her the creek was not the problem and it was a 1-in-100-year flood. (city staff (as reported by the delegate))
public: M.N. (Steinbach & Area Animal Rescue): the creek is choked with brush and backs up even in modest rain; the rescue followed all lot-grading rules and hired an engineer; its insurance renewal was at risk without a plan.
notes: That the Keating Drain cleanout is the channel beside 39 Keating Road is inferred from the location, not stated.

title: Georgetown residents' delegation: five backups, a door-to-door survey, and a call for answers and compensation
themes: residents; sanitary-sewer; lift-station; inflow-infiltration; compensation; independent-study; development
summary: M.R. spoke for Georgetown residents (Golfview Crescent and nearby streets). She said the 1988 line built for about 150 lots now also takes the Aquatic Centre, Granite Park and Clear Spring Greens (low-pressure system), and that backups coincided with each addition. Her survey of 83 homes found 47% backed up in 2024 and 69% in 2025, many with working backwater valves and sump pumps.
