She asked where the extra flow comes from, for proof if sump pumps are blamed, for engineering analysis, and what the city would do about compensation. Councillor Susan Penner (a neighbour) said council was committed to act next year; the mayor said her report would go into the stormwater drainage investigation for the study session.
status_detail: Council later rerouted the Clear Spring Greens low-pressure line (tender Jul 21, 2026), as residents had suggested. No answer on compensation was given at the meeting or later; no independent engineering analysis was commissioned (see 2026-independent-study-request).
figures: Survey of 83 homes: 39 (47%) backed up Sept 17, 2024; 58 (69%) Sept 12, 2025 (delegation; minutes Oct 21, 2025).
reasons: study-first: Residents' material to be added to the stormwater drainage investigation for the study session. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: M.R. (delegation, Georgetown): five backups since 2002; insurance lost after the second claim; asked 'What is the city going to do about compensation…?' and whether the 1988 line can carry the added load. Her claims about the causes are her own and unproven.
notes: Damian Penner's quote is medium confidence (speaker map).

title: Residents ask for an independent study of why Georgetown backs up; none commissioned
summary: Georgetown residents repeatedly asked for engineering analysis: on Oct 21, 2025 (no reply to their request for any engineer's analysis), Mar 17, 2026 (a study of the root cause), and Jul 21, 2026, when M.R. read an email from Adam Thiessen saying no outsourced study was done for the 2026 plan and asked again for a third-party study of the sewer system and Lift Station 1. Asked whether developers' consultants are independent, the City Manager said they work for the developer and are reviewed by the city. The mayor said studies are 'a valid point' and the city is doing what it can.
status_detail: No independent or third-party study was commissioned or promised in any recorded meeting to Nov 3, 2026. The climate risk assessment (Aug 2026) is city-wide and was not presented as a root-cause study.
reasons: already-doing: The city is already working on projects as fast as it can. (Mayor Earl Funk); engineering-standard: Development servicing is checked against city standards by city staff and the city engineer. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: M.R. (Georgetown): 'I want a third-party study'; G.R. asked 'What is causing the problem?'. These are residents' requests; no study has confirmed or ruled out their theories.
notes: The email M.R. read was from Adam Thiessen (staff); its wording is as she read it.

title: New 1,500 kW backup generator for Lift Station 1 bought early
summary: Because of long lead times, council approved buying the larger backup generator for the 2026 Lift Station 1 upgrade ahead of the main tender.
status_detail: Approved (R25-210); its cost is included in the Lift Station 1 budget awarded Mar 17, 2026.
figures: $670,600 plus taxes, Toromont Cat (R25-210; transcript 0:12:26).

title: First Street apartments approved over neighbours' sewer and stormwater questions
summary: At the hearing for a 31-unit development at 190-206 First Street, R.P. asked whether 1960s sewer lines could handle more than doubling the units, and J.G. asked about stormwater since First Street floods in heavy storms. The City Manager said First Street's underground services are on the long-term capital plan within 5 years but have no date, and that existing infrastructure is adequate. The mayor said drainage would be handled in the development agreement.
status_detail: Residents' concerns did not change the outcome: conditional use approved (R25-248) and variance approved (R25-249). First Street renewal remains unscheduled.
figures: 31 units (applicant, 0:29:00); First Street renewal 'within the next 5 years' (0:30:54).
reasons: not-grounds-to-block-development: Drainage is dealt with in the development agreement between developer and city engineer. (Mayor Earl Funk); engineering-standard: City engineer found existing infrastructure adequate. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: R.P. (185 First Street): sewer never upgraded in 20 years, lines from the 1960s; J.G. (226 First Street): First Street floods in heavy storms.
notes: The resident R.P. shares a surname with two councillors; he is a member of the public.

title: Millwork Drive sewer main replaced: 1965 concrete pipe upsized, tender under estimate
summary: Council asked the MWSB for 50% of the Millwork Drive sewer main project (Dec 16, 2025), then awarded the contract to replace about 800 m of 1965 concrete 450 mm pipe with 525 mm PVC between PTH 12 and the trunk line (Mar 3, 2026). The bid came in about $700,000 under the consultant's estimate. Councillors called sewer pipe the most basic job of a city.
status_detail: MWSB request R25-258; contract R26-050 to Friesen Hauling and Excavating. Completion not reported in a recorded meeting.
figures: Contract $1,462,540 plus taxes vs estimate $2,129,607 (transcript Mar 3, 2026, 0:10:41; R26-050).
reasons: already-doing: One of three projects on the capital plan since 2022. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
notes: The Dec 16, 2025 agenda item was introduced as 'Park Road West, Forest Main' but the resolution read was for Millwork Drive (minutes R25-258).

title: DFA denied again for 2025: council demands the criteria, gets a vague answer
summary: On Jan 20, 2026 the province again denied Disaster Financial Assistance, this time for the Sept 11, 2025 storm. The mayor called the criteria vague and council unanimously asked the province how the event was assessed and what the criteria are. Administration wrote to every applicant to report the denial. On Apr 21 Adam Thiessen reported back: the province judges insurability for the region as a whole first, does not count repeat events, and has no defined criteria for area or number of residents. Zwaagstra called it 'a political decision rather than one based on actual evidence'.
status_detail: Clarification requested (R26-020) and report received Apr 21, 2026 (no motion). Aid remained denied.
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Compensation for residents depends on the provincial DFA program; council's role is to press the province. (Mayor Earl Funk)

title: Park Road West force main contract awarded at $1.49M, well under estimate
summary: Council awarded the force main twinning contract, part of the $7.4M Park Road West project with the Lift Station 1 upgrade. Susan Penner tied it to the two floods; the mayor said it helps every property and 'will facilitate more growth'.
status_detail: Awarded to Southwood Ventures Inc. (R26-038). At least 50% to be funded by MWSB grant.
figures: $1,494,661.05 plus taxes (R26-038); engineer's estimate $2.4M; whole project estimate $7.4M (D. Penner, 0:28:26).
reasons: already-doing: Long-planned capacity project for the whole city. (Mayor Earl Funk)

title: Clear Spring Greens low-pressure sewer rerouted away from Golfview Crescent, without a study
summary: Council directed that the Clear Spring Greens low-pressure sewer, which discharged into the Golfview Crescent line, be extended along Park Road East to the PTH 12 North main. The City Manager said it was 'entirely council-initiated' in response to residents, not based on a study, and subject to the consultant finding no downstream harm. Residents welcomed it but worried it may not be the root cause. The tender came in far under estimate in July.
status_detail: Contract awarded Jul 21, 2026 to Beaver Sewer & Water Services (R26-149), to be finished in the 2026 season. Completion and any before/after flow data were not reported in recorded meetings.
figures: $396,500 plus taxes vs consultant's estimate $614,000 (transcript Jul 21, 2026, 1:19:16; R26-149).
public: M.R. asked whether an engineer recommended the reroute and said 'We worry that that might not be the root cause.' Georgetown residents had raised the Clear Spring Greens connection in their Oct 21, 2025 delegation.

title: 2026 budget and flood mitigation plan: over $20M for wastewater, mostly projects planned since 2022
themes: capital-work; sanitary-sewer; lift-station; drainage; sump-pump; communication
summary: At the 2026 financial plan hearing the City Manager presented the flood mitigation plan council drafted after the storms (November 2025 study session). 2025 steps: climate risk assessment, a $30,000 Clear Spring Greens drainage fix, sewer and storm camera programs, drain maintenance, DFA work, storm-damage mapping, the Keating Drain cleanout, and recalibrating pumps. 2026: three capital projects (Millwork Drive main, force main twinning, Lift Station 1, about $8-9M) that were on the plan since 2022, plus PTH 52 East and Park Road East drainage, a sump pump by-law review with private-property inspections, and the Clear Spring Greens reroute. A drainage master plan, basement-depth policy, drain bypass or detention concept and flow sensors were listed only as possible future projects. The budget passed unanimously with no mill-rate increase.
status_detail: Budget adopted (R26-058). The capital projects were tendered and the by-law passed in 2026; the future items (drainage master plan, flow sensors, detention plan) were not funded. On Apr 7, 2026 the City Manager said 2026's focus was 'mostly capital projects that had already been initiated well prior to this year'.
figures: Capital program $35.8M; mill rate 14.4 unchanged; three projects about $8-9M (transcript 0:17:48); 'over $20 million' for wastewater (D. Penner 0:38:22); sanitary televising just over $100,000/yr, storm televising about $60,000/yr, major drains $50,000/yr; Keating Drain cleanout and Clear Spring Greens drainage about $30,000 each.
reasons: already-doing: Core projects were already on the capital plan since 2022. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); study-first: More to come once the climate risk assessment is done. (Mayor Earl Funk); cost: Done with no tax increase and 5-year debt. (Damian Penner)
public: M.R. asked how the solutions were chosen, whether engineers recommended them, when they would take effect, and whether studies would be public; she asked for a study of the root cause.
notes: The November 2025 study session and the Mar 10, 2026 committee meeting were not recorded.

title: Land Drainage By-law 2274 replaces the sump pump by-law, with inspections and fines
summary: After the flood plan called for a review of Sump Pump By-law 1674 and inspections of private sewer, sump pit and septic installations, council gave first reading to a broader Land Drainage By-law on May 19, 2026 and passed it on Aug 4, along with administrative penalties (By-law 2282). It lets the city inspect private property and require compliance; older homes can be exempted case by case so owners are not penalized for adding backup protection. Inspections were to start later that summer, with advice to residents still being worked out.
status_detail: By-law 2274: first reading May 19 (R26-102; no video), second and third Aug 4 (R26-162, R26-163). Penalty By-law 2282 (R26-164, R26-165). No subsidy for disconnection or backwater valves was discussed. Inspection results not reported.
figures: Fine amounts are in By-law 2282 (agenda package p. 121); not stated in the meeting.
reasons: private-property: Sump pumps and private drainage must not put stormwater into the sewer. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); fairness-precedent: Older homes exempted case by case so as not to penalize backup protection. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: At the Apr 7, 2026 hearing residents said sump pump water in the sewer was a main cause of backups (unproven); in July residents said they had already installed sump pumps and backwater valves at their own cost.
mover: Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Damian Penner; Damian Penner
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert; Jake Hiebert; Jake Hiebert
notes: May 19, 2026 meeting (first reading) has no transcript.

title: Lift Station 1 upgrade awarded: pumping capacity to rise from 482 to 843 L/s
summary: Council awarded the Lift Station 1 building upgrade on Park Road West, the third core project. Only one bid came in, 2% under the engineer's estimate. Design pumping capacity rises from 482 to 843 litres per second.
status_detail: Awarded to Penn-Co Construction (R26-060). Councillors said in July it would be done that summer; completion not confirmed in a recorded meeting.
figures: $4,326,078.39 plus taxes; estimate $4,636,065; 482 to 843 L/s (transcript 1:52:47-1:53:20; R26-060). Funding: MWSB grant, utility reserve, utility debt.
reasons: already-doing: On the capital plan since 2022. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
notes: The existing report links the award at 1:52:10 (item introduction).

title: McKenzie Avenue 48-unit rezoning approved; neighbours cite backups, staff blame a blockage
summary: At the hearing for By-law 2273 (492-506 McKenzie, 48 units), neighbours with a petition said their basements flooded with sewage in 2024 and 2025. A.R., a utilities manager for another town, described undersized storm sewers and manholes under water letting street water into the sewer; P.K., who said he helped design parts of the system, said uncontrolled sump pump discharge from Deerfield and Clear Spring Greens overwhelmed it and asked that density wait until that is fixed. The City Manager said 10-12 nearby properties were affected in 2025, the backup was caused by a blockage found after the storm, and the engineer saw no sewer capacity concern. The mayor said sump pump by-law compliance work is under way.
status_detail: Residents' request to refuse or wait was not adopted: second reading carried unanimously (R26-068); third reading Sept 1, 2026 (R26-184).
figures: 48 units; 10-12 properties affected nearby in 2025 (Warkentin, 1:02:09).
reasons: not-grounds-to-block-development: Local backup was from a blockage unrelated to the number of units. (Michael Zwaagstra); engineering-standard: City engineer reported no sewer main capacity concern. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); already-doing: Sump pump by-law work and budget projects under way. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Residents (H.K., A.R., P.K., J.D., B.D., C.V.) cited 2024/2025 sewage backups, undersized street drainage, and sump pumps in the sewer. P.K.'s claim that sump pumps from Deerfield and Clear Spring Greens caused the Georgetown and McKenzie backups is his opinion and unproven.

title: City moves to take over the Manning Canal from the province
summary: Council approved a memorandum of understanding to begin transferring the Manning Canal, the last provincially controlled drain through the city, to city jurisdiction after talks since 2022. The mayor said the canal 'does not work very well' in severe rain. On Aug 4, 2026 council passed a plan-of-works by-law (2227) to rebuild a canal segment through the Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard development.
status_detail: MOU approved (R26-081); formal transfer needs a provincial Lieutenant Governor in Council decision, not reported. By-law 2227 passed (R26-152, R26-160, R26-161).
mover: Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert; Bill Hiebert
seconder: Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner; Jac Siemens

title: Council asks the province to reopen Steinbach's 2024 and 2025 DFA files after rules eased for other rural floods
summary: After Premier Kinew said in June 2026 that the province would not let posted DFA rules stand in the way of helping rural flood victims, the mayor asked council to write for Steinbach's claims to be reopened. Zwaagstra moved a formal request to reconsider, reopen and approve the 2024 and 2025 applications; members said Steinbach only wants to be treated fairly. The mayor recounted being told on radio that Steinbach needs better insurance brokers.
status_detail: Resolution carried (R26-129). No provincial response was reported in later recorded meetings (to Nov 3, 2026).
reasons: provincial-responsibility: Province should apply the same relaxed rules to Steinbach residents. (Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Six-storey seniors building near Georgetown approved 6-1 after a hearing dominated by flooding
themes: development; sanitary-sewer; drainage; overland-flooding; residents; independent-study
summary: Bridgepark Manor asked for six storeys and reduced parking at 290 Stone Bridge Crossing, already zoned for three. Neighbours from Georgetown, Granite Park, Stone Bridge Crossing and Albert Street, many flooded repeatedly, asked whether sewer and drainage could take more load and for third-party review. The mayor said the hearing was about height and parking; the City Manager said developers' consultants work for the developer, their plans are checked against city standards, and no system handles storms beyond 1-in-100. Zwaagstra said the site is not in the Georgetown sewer catchment; Susan and Damian Penner said council can do both growth and flood work. Siemens moved to deny (no seconder), then voted against on height.
status_detail: Residents' request to refuse was not adopted: variance approved 6-1 with parking at 1.25 per unit (R26-147; against: Siemens, on height).
figures: 81 suites planned; 220 people on a waiting list (S. Penner, 0:59:04); parking 1.25/unit.
reasons: not-grounds-to-block-development: Site is not in the Georgetown catchment; can't refuse because of another area's flooding. (Michael Zwaagstra); not-grounds-to-block-development: Can't stop development until residents feel okay. (Damian Penner); already-doing: Lift station doubling and bigger pipes under way; growth and flood work at once. (Susan Penner); extreme-storm: No system anywhere handles storms beyond 1-in-100. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager)); engineering-standard: Development servicing reviewed against city standards. (Troy Warkentin (City Manager))
public: M.R., B.K., D.J., D.F., M.N. and G.R. described repeated flooding (some 'five plus' times), lost insurance and falling home values, and asked for third-party review. M.R.'s remark about favouritism in local business was called speculation by the mayor; it is unproven.
notes: The transcript of this meeting starts partway into M.R.'s hearing remarks (0:00:00).

title: Williams Creek subdivision approved; neighbours say existing drainage was never fixed
summary: At the hearing for 155 homes south of Loewen Boulevard (By-law 2283 and subdivision), S.B. and G.W., neighbours to the south, said water already sits in their yards and garages, that problems began when the Wyndham development started, and that city visits had not fixed it; they asked to see the drainage design first. The applicant (M.J.) said a 30-foot concrete-bottom swale would help them. The mayor said their problem seemed isolated to their properties and drainage would be handled in the development agreement; councillors trusted the engineering department.
status_detail: Request to settle drainage before approval not adopted: second reading R26-156 and subdivision R26-157 carried unanimously. Neighbours' existing drainage problem left with staff; no fix reported.
figures: About 74 acres, 155 homes (J./B. Hiebert, 0:50:58); 30-foot public reserve with concrete-bottom swale.
reasons: engineering-standard: Faith in the engineering department and lot levels set in development agreements. (Jac Siemens); private-property: Neighbours' problem 'more or less obviously isolated on your properties'. (Mayor Earl Funk); not-grounds-to-block-development: Plan meets the zoning by-law; no ad hoc rules. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: S.B. (86 Ashgrove Lane) and G.W. (Wyndham Estate Drive) described standing water and neighbours' flood damage of $60,000-70,000; they blame the Wyndham development (unproven).
notes: The applicant's representative, M.J., is a member of the public.

title: Homeowners sue the city over repeated sewer backups (pending; not discussed at council)
summary: According to news reports cited in the existing report (CTV News, Aug 19, 2026; SteinbachOnline), homeowners filed a lawsuit against the city in Manitoba's Court of King's Bench on Aug 13, 2026, alleging negligence and nuisance over repeated sewer backups, including late activation of auxiliary pumps and tying new subdivisions into a strained line. These are allegations; none has been proven.
status_detail: Pending. The suit did not come up in any recorded council meeting from Aug 4 to Nov 3, 2026.
figures: Plaintiffs: 13 per SteinbachOnline, 22 per CTV (news reports; not verified against the court filing).
reasons: legal-advice: Council has not spoken about the suit in public meetings; litigation may limit comment. ((not stated))
public: Allegations by homeowners in the lawsuit are unproven.
notes: Not verified against the court filing; details from the existing report's sources.

title: 58 Giesbrecht rezoning approved; 'we can't build pipes big enough'
summary: Neighbours of a 12-unit rezoning at 58 Giesbrecht Street said the street already floods 'like a river' in heavy rain. The mayor and the applicant said new development must hold water on site and release it slowly, so infill often improves drainage. Siemens said the city cannot afford pipes big enough for every storm, so streets carry water in torrential rain.
status_detail: Second reading carried unanimously (R26-179). No street drainage fix for Giesbrecht was discussed.
figures: 12 units, 2 storeys.
reasons: cost: Pipes big enough for every storm are not financially feasible. (Jac Siemens); engineering-standard: On-site retention in the development agreement. (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: G.W. (30 Giesbrecht) and K.V. (Westview Place) described street flooding and asked the city to find another solution.
notes: G.W. here is a different resident from G.W. at the Aug 4 Williams Creek hearing.
